log.reason: The issue is a 6-day port-congestion delay escalated as Severity 1 because of production risk, so the governing rule would be a delay-notification or escalation procedure. None of the candidates covers that. SOP-01-C3.2 sets Arrival Notice timing and content, not delay escalation. SOP-04-C4.1 covers damage or shortage claims. SOP-01-C1.2 only defines scope. SOP-03-C2.1 covers the contract free time table.

The issue is the consignee's request for priority customs clearance and the resulting release. None of the candidate clauses sets an obligation about expediting or prioritising clearance. C5.2 covers D/O requests, C3.2 the Arrival Notice timing, C5.1 physical inspection notices (no inspection is mentioned) and C6.1 POD collection, so none of them governs this case.

The decision is about handling a vessel delay: accepting it without re-routing and sending daily ETA updates. None of the candidates set an obligation on delay handling or ETA updates. SOP-01-C3.2 covers the timing and content of the Arrival Notice, not delay management. The POD, claim notice and empty-return clauses deal with unrelated post-delivery matters.

A missing health certificate leaves the document set incomplete, so the broker could not file. SOP-01-C4.1 requires the Import Operator to forward a complete document set to the customs broker at least 2 working days before ETA, and says incomplete sets do not meet this requirement. None of the other clauses fits: SOP-05-C2.1 covers how instructions are sent, SOP-03-C2.1 covers free time, and SOP-01-C3.1 covers checking that HBL and MBL data match.

The decision is about when to file the import declaration so the cargo clears before free time runs out. None of the candidates sets a rule for declaration filing, timing or free-time management. The other clauses cover pre-alert review, the Arrival Notice, written instructions to brokers and truckers, and email subject lines, so none governs this case.

The demurrage arose because the extension request came too late and Pacific Star refused it. SOP-03-C4.2 directly governs this: it requires extension requests at least 2 working days before free-time expiry and warns against relying on post-expiry requests. Nothing suggests the invoice contradicts the recorded free time, so the dispute clause (C4.4) does not apply. The free-time table (C2.1) and recording clause (C2.2) are not the obligation at issue.

The extension was refused because the request was sent on the expiry day. SOP-03-C4.2 requires extension requests to be sent at least 2 working days before free time expires, so it is the rule that was breached. C4.1 covers the general duty to request an extension in writing, not its timing. C2.1 sets free-time lengths and C4.4 covers invoice disputes, so neither applies.

The decision splits the demurrage, with Meridian absorbing part and billing the rest to the consignee. SOP-03-C4.3 governs demurrage charge allocation: consignee-caused demurrage is billed to the consignee, Meridian-caused demurrage is absorbed only with Import Team Lead approval, and each absorption must be recorded. The other clauses cover free-time values, procedure scope and broker allocation, none of which is about this decision.

The issue is a customs physical inspection that passed, followed by release. None of the candidate clauses sets an obligation about customs inspection itself. The D/O clauses (SOP-01-C5.2, SOP-02-C2.4) govern requesting the D/O, the written-instruction clause (SOP-05-C2.1) governs instructing brokers and truckers, and SOP-01-C3.2 governs the Arrival Notice. None of those actions is the subject of this issue.

This is a customs documentary query about the import licence, and the consignee has to supply a copy. None of the candidates governs it. SOP-01-C5.1 covers notifying the consignee when a shipment is selected for physical inspection, but the issue does not say the inspection is physical. SOP-01-C3.1 (pre-alert review) and SOP-05-C2.1 (written instructions to brokers and truckers) do not apply. SOP-01-C4.2 is about HS code verification, not licences.

The decision is about who from Meridian Freight attends the physical inspection. SOP-01-C5.1 covers physical inspection, but its obligations are only to notify the consignee within 1 working day and to record the inspection in the file; it says nothing about attending. The other clauses (delivery order, document collection, proof of delivery) are unrelated, so no candidate governs this case.

The decision is about who sends the import licence copy to customs to resolve a licence-number query. None of the candidates governs that. SOP-05-C2.1 covers instructing brokers and truckers. SOP-01-C3.1 covers pre-alert review and SOP-01-C3.2 covers the Arrival Notice to the consignee. SOP-02-C2.1's subject-line rule applies to every shipment email, but it sets formatting, not whether or how documents go to customs.

The broker filed under an HS code that differed from the consignee's import history (8482.99 instead of 8482.10), and no written confirmation was obtained beforehand. SOP-01-C4.2 directly covers this: it requires the operator to cross-check the HS code against import history and to confirm any change in writing with the consignee before filing. The other clauses cover e-mail instruction format, subject lines and pre-alert data matching, which are not at issue here.

The decision is about whether to change the HS code. SOP-01-C4.2 is the only clause on HS code verification and on changing an HS code, so it governs. Keeping the filed code 8482.99 means no change is made. The other clauses do not apply: pre-alert review, MBL/HBL subject-line rules and B/L amendments are not about customs HS code classification.

SOP-01-C4.2 requires that any HS code change be confirmed in writing before the declaration is filed, which is the rule breached here. SOP-05-C3.2 covers recording non-conformances against a vendor, which is the action Minseo Park took against the broker. The manifest correction and written instruction clauses do not address this situation.

The D/O was requested before the telex release from origin had been confirmed, so the carrier refused it. SOP-02-C2.4 forbids sending a D/O request until the original B/L surrender or telex release is confirmed and recorded. SOP-01-C5.2 likewise allows a D/O request only once the telex release (and customs release) is confirmed. SOP-02-C2.3 covers how a telex release replaces the original B/L and how to file it, not when a D/O may be requested. SOP-03-C2.1 covers free time and is unrelated.

The decision absorbs demurrage caused by Meridian's own error instead of billing the consignee. SOP-03-C4.3 directly governs this: absorption needs Import Team Lead approval and must be recorded as a cost-absorption decision. The other clauses cover email subject lines, procedure scope and vendor approval, so none of them sets an obligation for this decision.

The decision assigns a specific customs broker (Kim & Park Customs Services, Busan office) to Blue Harbor Foods reefer imports. That is a customer-to-broker allocation, which SOP-05-C1.2's broker allocation table governs. SOP-05-C1.1 covers checking the approved vendor list before instructing any vendor; it does not decide which broker serves which customer. SOP-03-C2.1 covers free time, and SOP-05-C2.1 covers the format of written instructions; neither applies here.

The case is wet damage noted at delivery. SOP-04-C4.1 governs because the Import Operator must notify the carrier in writing within 3 days of delivery to preserve recourse. SOP-04-C4.2 governs because photos and delivery receipt remarks are required before any settlement discussion. Since the expected claim exceeds USD 10,000, a survey report is also required. SOP-04-C1.1 and SOP-04-C1.2 are generic rules on classifying exceptions, not the claim-specific obligations at issue. C1.2's severity rule could arguably apply, since any exception over USD 500 is Severity 1, but under a strict reading it is not directly about this damage claim. C1.1's category table is cut off and does not visibly include cargo damage.

The decision covers appointing a surveyor, pursuing the wet damage claim and sending weekly updates to the consignee. SOP-04-C4.1 only requires written notice to the carrier within 3 days of delivery, which is not what was decided here. The other three clauses cover demurrage, free-time reminders and D&D invoice disputes, so none of them applies.

The decision is a handover of a claim file before staff leave. None of the candidates covers claim handling or staff handover. SOP-02-C2.1 covers email subject lines, SOP-05-C2.1 covers instructions to brokers and truckers, SOP-01-C3.1 covers pre-alert review, and SOP-01-C4.2 covers HS code verification.

The issue only states the business urgency: the consignee's line stops unless clearance and delivery happen the same day. None of the candidate clauses sets an obligation about expedited or same-day handling. The D/O clauses (SOP-01-C5.2, SOP-02-C2.4) would only govern if the case involved a D/O request decision, which the issue does not mention. The Arrival Notice (SOP-01-C3.2) and pre-alert review (SOP-01-C3.1) clauses deal with earlier stages and do not apply.

Harbor Gate's USD 150 expedite fee is a vendor charge outside the annual rate sheet. SOP-05-C2.2 requires a quotation approved by the Import Team Lead before such a service is performed, and bars the operator from authorising the vendor until then. The other clauses cover free time, arrival notices and email subject lines, so none of them governs accepting an extra vendor charge.

The detention charge depends on whether the empty was returned within the contract free time. SOP-03-C2.1 sets that free time (7 days for Hanseatic Marine Lines), so it governs the check of this invoice. SOP-03-C5.1 only covers recording the trucker's written return confirmation, not the free-time or detention assessment. The SOP-01 clauses on the Arrival Notice and POD are unrelated.

The issue is a missed 48-hour written escalation to the Import Team Lead, which is exactly what SOP-04 3.1 requires for Severity 1 exceptions. The other clauses do not fit. They cover disputing contradictory D&D invoices, recording empty return dates, and evidence collection before a damage settlement, and none of these is about escalation timing.

None of the candidates directly governs this decision. The dispute rests on typhoon terminal-closure days and on recharging the trucker for its dispatch backlog. SOP-03-C4.4 only covers invoices that contradict the recorded free time, which is not the basis here. C2.1 (free-time table), C5.1 (empty return confirmation) and SOP-04-C4.1 (cargo damage notice) do not address allocating detention or disputing force-majeure days.

The decision is an internal handover of a detention dispute to another staff member before a departure. None of the candidate clauses sets any rule about handover or reassigning work. SOP-03-C4.4 covers the dispute itself (the 7-day deadline and the free-time reference), not who handles it. The other three clauses cover D/O requests, broker allocation and the free-time table, none of which apply here.

The decision is an internal handover of trucker billing (a detention debit note to Rapid Haul Logistics). None of the candidates covers handovers or billing a trucker for detention. SOP-03-C4.4 covers disputing carrier D&D invoices, SOP-03-C2.1 covers applying contract free time, SOP-03-C5.1 covers recording the trucker's empty-return confirmation, and SOP-01-C5.3 covers trucking booking timing.

The decision is about a manifest correction filed after arrival (post-ATA). SOP-02-C3.2 requires manifest corrections to be filed before ATA and sends late corrections to the Import Team Lead, so it is the governing clause. The B/L amendment clause (C3.1), the claim notice clause (C4.1) and the telex release clause (C2.3) deal with other matters.

The decision is a staff handover: Jiwoo Han reassigning a filing task to Hoon Jang before her leave. None of the candidate clauses covers task handover or reassignment between operators. SOP-02-C3.2 concerns the deadline for filing manifest corrections before ATA, not who files them or how duties are delegated. The other clauses cover telex release, D/O requests and B/L amendments, which are unrelated.

The issue is only that the S-016 detention invoice is still unsettled, so the incident stays on the open list in the KPI report. None of the candidates covers tracking or reporting open D&D incidents. C4.4 applies only when an invoice contradicts the recorded free time, which is not stated here. C5.1 covers recording the empty return date. C2.2 covers recording the free-time expiry date. C1.2 is a definition of demurrage versus detention.

The decision changes Pacific Star's reefer free time at Busan, which is a contract free-time value. SOP-03-C2.1 holds the contract free time table the operator must apply, so it is the clause the change updates. SOP-03-C1.1 only defines free time and does not set carrier values. The watch-list clause (SOP-03-C3.1) and the POD clause (SOP-01-C6.1) are not directly about this change.

This decision is an internal handover of who maintains the free-time table. C2.1 only requires the Import Operator to apply the contract free times in the table; it says nothing about who updates or owns the table. C2.2, C3.2 and C4.4 cover recording expiry dates, consignee reminders and disputes, none of which apply here. No candidate clause directly governs this handover.

SOP-05-C3.2 governs this case. It requires vendor errors to be recorded and discussed with the vendor, and it triggers an allocation review once non-conformances accumulate in a quarter. SOP-05-C3.1 sets up the quarterly review, but its required scope (clearance lead time and trucker on-time rate) does not cover non-conformances. SOP-01-C4.2 is about the operator's own HS-code check, not vendor review. SOP-05-C2.1 is about written instructions and does not apply.

The decision is about discussing a recorded vendor non-conformance with the broker. SOP-05-C3.2 requires that vendor errors be recorded and discussed with the vendor concerned. The HS-code verification, broker allocation and written-instruction clauses cover operational steps, not handling vendor non-conformance.

This is a cargo damage claim against the carrier. SOP-04 4.1 requires written claim notice to the carrier to preserve recourse, which covers the formal claim to Orient Container Line. SOP-04 4.2 requires a survey report for higher-value claims before settlement, which covers the surveyor report. The empty-return and POD clauses do not address damage claims.

The issue is an open dispute with the carrier's D&D desk over detention charges. SOP-03-C4.4 directly governs disputing D&D charges with the carrier. It requires the dispute to be raised within 7 days of the invoice and to reference the recorded free-time expiry. The other clauses do not cover the dispute itself: C1.2 only defines the demurrage/detention distinction, C5.1 covers recording the empty return date, and C4.1 covers extension requests for foreseeable delays.

None of the candidates directly governs this case. The issue is filing the carrier's written confirmation of a manifest correction in the shipment's document register. SOP-02-C3.2 covers filing the manifest correction itself at destination before ATA and escalating if that is late; it says nothing about recording carrier confirmations. C3.1 covers B/L amendments, and C2.3 and C2.4 cover telex release and B/L release confirmations, so none of them fits.

The decision reassigns who owns the open Daehan Precision and Seoul Medica import files. SOP-01-C2.1 is the only candidate about this: each import file must have an Import Operator owner who is the single point of contact until delivery. The D/O, broker-instruction and broker-allocation clauses cover operational steps, not file ownership or handover.
